utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Ms. Pack.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I wanted to correct a matter on the transcript for the 30th of September. At transcript pages 47797 to 98, in answering Your Honour's question concerning the Defence brief paragraph 2549, I said the only individual -- that only individual C on Karadzic's list had been included in Dusan Janc's figure of 5977 identified individuals in the Srebrenica graves. In fact, individual D is also included in that figure. And for that I refer you to P4771, page 119, entry 132, and page 279, entry 20. And also Janc's testimony at T26949 to 51 and 26965, and P4771, page 6. And, Your Honours, similar to C, KDZ045 only heard but did not see that D was killed in the woods. And the cite is KDZ045, and the transcript reference is 22678. I'm very grateful. That's the only matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pack. Yes, Mr. Karadzic -- oh, yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'll be addressing you at the beginning of this session. So first of all, let me first answer the Trial Chamber's questions that were communicated to us last Friday by your Legal Officer. Most of the questions were directed to the Prosecution and I'll only address those that were expressly directed to us. But should the Trial Chamber wish to hear our position on any of the questions posed to the Prosecution, please let us know and Dr. Karadzic or I would be happy to address those questions. I think that Dr. Karadzic has already addressed your question number 2 at least twice yesterday concerning efforts by Bosnian Serb authorities to control paramilitaries. With respect to question 7 concerning two victims from Brcko, you addressed your question to the Prosecution but you asked us on Tuesday whether we had any issue with the Prosecution's explanation. We do. Now, here's your question. You asked with respect to Brcko that the Chamber had received death certificates for P4411, P4412, from the bar table, which in the Prosecution's submission were linked to incident B5.1. But there appears to be no other evidence linking these persons to the killing incident. And you asked does the Prosecution have any submission in this regard. And Mr. Tieger conceded that there was no evidence that the first victim died at Luka camp as charged in scheduled incident B5.1, but this is what he said with respect to the second victim. He said that the victim was among the victims buried in a mass grave in Brcko which is listed in Avlijas's 22 October report, P1607. And he said that Ristanic had agreed and testified that the victims in that report were non-Serb civilians who were killed in Brcko, including at Luka camp and similar places. And he cited P3023, paragraphs 220 to 223. But let's look at those exhibits. P1607, the report from Avlijas, says simply that these people died during combat activities in Brcko. P3023 is the amalgamated statement of the Prosecution witness Mr. Ristanic. At paragraph 221, he stated that: "Those were people who were killed by Jelesic and that sort of people and some of those people actually died in combat activity." Then in paragraph 222 he was asked: "It's true, though, isn't it that they have been killed and executed in and around Brcko including places like camp Luka, places in and around the police station and other notorious killing sites?" And he said: "Yes." Now, your question was about schedule B5.1, which charges the killing of a number of men in Luka camp between the 8th of May and the 6th of June, 1992. So do these two exhibits prove that the second victim was killed in Luka camp? Absolutely not. There's clearly insufficient evidence to conclude that the victims died at Luka prison which is the only scheduled incident for Brcko. Now, for question number 9, you've asked us in essence whether our submissions on Counts 9 and 10 were intended to apply to alleged murders in Sarajevo charged in Counts 5 and 6. And the answer is yes. Finally, in question 14, you've asked us about the impact of the Prosecution's disclosure violations on any sentence that might be imposed upon Dr. Karadzic if he's convicted. As you know, on 73 occasions so far in this case you've made a finding that the Prosecution has violated its disclosure obligations. On some occasions you recessed the trial for several months to give the Defence time to prepare based upon the late disclosure. And you've asked us whether -- you've asked us why those delays in Dr. Karadzic's trial ought to result in a reduction of his sentence when he would be given credit for the time he's served during such delays in any event. However, it's our position that there is no correlation between the two. In those cases in which the Appeals Chamber or Trial Chamber have reduced a sentence for undue delay, the defendant has been given credit for the time served in any event. This includes the Barayagwiza case, known as the Prosecutor versus Nahimana at the ICTR, involving a delay in bringing the accused before a judge after his arrest in Cameroon, and the Kajelijeli case, also from the ICTR, involving a delay in bringing the accused before a judge after his arrest in Benin. Both received significant sentence reductions for the violation of their rights in addition to the credit for the time that they'd served. We say that it's important for the Trial Chamber to provide a remedy for the massive violations of the Prosecution's disclosure obligations, not only to benefit Dr. Karadzic, but to send a clear message to this and future Prosecution teams that such violations will not be tolerated. I would like now to talk to you about genocide. It's my respectful submission that Dr. Karadzic is not guilty of the genocide charges in Count 1 and 2 of the indictment. Let's look at the definition of genocide. It's Article 4 of the ICTY Statute. And it means "any of the following acts committed with the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group, as such ..." And the pertinent acts for our case is: "Killing members of the group"; Causing them serious bodily or mental harm; or "Deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part." But it's the special intent to destroy the group that distinguishes genocide from other serious crimes such as extermination and persecution. The Appeals Chamber has held that genocide is one of the worst crimes known to humankind and its gravity is reflected in the stringent requirement of specific intent. Convictions for genocide can be entered only when that intent has been unequivocally established. And that's the Krstic appeals judgement at paragraph 134. Now, Count 1 charges Dr. Karadzic with genocide in seven municipalities during 1992: Bratunac, Foca, Kljuc, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Vlasenica, and Zvornik. After the Prosecution had presented all of its evidence, this Trial Chamber ruled that there was no evidence upon which a reasonable trier of fact could find that the acts of killing, serious bodily or mental harm, and conditions of life inflicted on the Bosnian Muslims and/or the Bosnian Croats in the municipalities were perpetrated with the intent to destroy required for genocide. And it's our submission that nothing has occurred which would cause the Chamber to change its mind about the Prosecution's evidence. One thing that did occur was that the Appeals Chamber reversed the decision of the Trial Chamber and held that there was some evidence on the record which, taken at its highest, could support a finding of an intent to destroy on behalf of Dr. Karadzic and other members of the alleged joint criminal enterprise. The first question then is: What is the impact of the Appeals Chamber's judgement on the decision to be made by the Trial Chamber at the end of the case? The Appeals Chamber itself emphasised that a judgement of acquittal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, bearing in mind the translation, if you could slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber itself emphasised that a judgement of acquittal at the end of the Prosecution case should only be entered when there was no evidence capable of supporting a conviction, that its conclusions regarding evidence before the Trial Chamber are taken at the highest, and that the question of whether the evidence would meet the standard of beyond a reasonable doubt remained open. It's our submission that the Prosecutor's evidence, while sufficient to overcome a motion for judgement of acquittal at the end of its own case, is insufficient to sustain a conviction requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt. And it's useful to look briefly at the evidence that the Appeals Chamber cited as examples of possible genocidal intent. It specifically referred to evidence of Prosecution Witness KDZ051, a Bosnian Muslim detained in Veljko Vlahovic school in Rogatica, who claimed that he was told by Sveto Veselinovic, a Bosnian Serb municipal leader, that during meetings with Dr. Karadzic it had been decided that one-third of the Muslims would be killed, one-third would be converted to the Orthodox religion, and one-third would leave on their own. Now, understandably in its final brief, the Prosecution no longer relies on this hearsay evidence to establish genocidal intent. This is Sveto Veselinovic. He came and testified during the defence case. He said that he was never at the Veljko Vlahovic school, he never made such a statement, and that he never heard Dr. Karadzic make such a statement. Therefore, the evidence from Witness KDZ051 cannot support a finding of genocidal intent beyond a reasonable doubt. The Appeals Chamber also relied upon a statement made at the Bosnian Serb Assembly on the 24th-26th of July, 1992, by Dr. Karadzic that there was some truth to what had been said presumably by a deputy named Miladin Nedic. Mr. Nedic had said that "the Muslims have been planted to us as a people whose executioners we are to be." Now, while one reasonable inference from this evidence is that Dr. Karadzic found some truth in the idea that European governments were trying to manipulate the Serbs, which was the thrust of Nedic's remarks, in fact Mr. Nedic came and testified during the Defence case. He testified that he in no way advocated genocide against the Muslims. If he didn't understand it that way, how could Dr. Karadzic? The Appeals Chamber also cited to statements made by Dr. Karadzic about what would happen if the war started in Bosnia. These statements are now what the Prosecution relies on to prove his genocidal intent. They include intercepted conversations in September and October 1991 with Momcilo Krajisnik, Gojko Dogo, and an unknown person from the Krajina, where Dr. Karadzic says that if the war starts in Bosnia, the Muslims would disappear. Dr. Karadzic made a similar statement at the Bosnian Assembly session of 15 October 1991, where he said that the Muslims were inviting a highway of hell and possible extinction because the Muslim people would not be able to defend itself if war broke out. It's our submission that it's a more reasonable inference from the context of these statements that Dr. Karadzic was trying to convince the Muslims not to start a war and to reach a peaceful solution, not making a public and private call for the extermination of the Bosnian Muslims as such. You alluded to this interpretation in your decision at the end of the Prosecution's case, when you found that notwithstanding these statements, there was no evidence of genocidal intent. And you were not alone. These very same statements were admitted into evidence in the Brdjanin and Krajisnik cases. This is a table showing the exhibit numbers of these statements in our case, the Krajisnik case, and the Brdjanin case. And the Trial Chambers in those cases unanimously held that these statements were not indicative of genocidal intent. This same evidence was also considered by the International Court of Justice in the case of Bosnia versus Serbia. That court, too, found that a pattern of conduct on the part of the leadership of Republika Srpska from which genocidal intent could be inferred had not been established. As you know, at this stage of the case the Prosecution has the burden of proving that an intention to destroy the Bosnian Muslims or Croats is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence. And while the Trial Chamber is not bound by the decisions in these other cases, although based on the same evidence, they demonstrate that one reasonable inference from the evidence before this Trial Chamber is that Dr. Karadzic's remarks were made to avoid war and not to promote genocide. In fact, you took judicial notice of 625 adjudicated facts from the Krajisnik case and 301 adjudicated facts from the Brdjanin case. You had sufficient confidence in the conclusions of those Chambers to reliably import those findings into our case. Would it not be incongruous, if not incomprehensible, for you to now find that their conclusion on the same evidence that Dr. Karadzic and the Bosnian Serb leadership had no genocidal intent was not even a reasonable one? For all of those reasons, I respectfully submit that Dr. Karadzic is not guilty of genocide, as charged in Count 1 of the indictment. You can find a more detailed analysis of the evidence, municipality by municipality, witness by witness, in the respondent's brief that we filed before the Appeals Chamber on the 5th of November, 2012. Now, that filing also acknowledges that crimes such as murder and infliction of serious harm, were committed during the 1992 events in the municipalities of Bosnia. And I would be remiss in concluding this submission if I did not at the same time acknowledge that there were indeed many innocent victims of these crimes. A finding by the Trial Chamber, like the findings of the Trial Chambers in Stakic, Brdjanin, and Krajisnik cases, and the International Court of Justice, that genocide was not committed in the municipalities of Bosnia in 1992 in no way diminishes the suffering of the victims or what they or their families endured during that terrible time. It simply reflects that the legal requirements for this very specific crime, requiring a very specific intent to destroy the group as such, have not been met. Even after what happened to the Jews in the Holocaust, the Supreme Court of Israel found Adolf Eichmann not guilty of genocide for crimes in the two-year period where the Jews were deported, rather than exterminated. What happened in Bosnia in 1992, while awful, was not genocide and Dr. Karadzic should likewise be found not guilty of Count 1. I would like to now turn to Count 2 and Dr. Karadzic's individual responsibility for genocide in connection with the July 1995 Srebrenica events. And this is a matter of life or death. If you're convinced that Dr. Karadzic planned or ordered the execution of thousands of prisoners from Srebrenica as part of some joint criminal enterprise with General Mladic, as the Prosecution claims, then you should give him a sentence that ensures that he too dies as a prisoner --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- like those who died on the fields of Branjevo Farm, Petkovci dam, or near the Orahovac school. But you would be doing a great injustice. Because the truth is that Radovan Karadzic never planned or ordered these executions. And if you agree to the legal lynching of Radovan Karadzic urged upon you by the Prosecution, an innocent man will have been convicted of a crime he did not commit. And I am here to try to convince you, with all of the force that I can muster while speaking slowly for the interpreters, not to do that. I am passionate in this. We have put everything into our final brief that could possibly explain and deal with the issue of Dr. Karadzic's responsibility for genocide at Srebrenica as charged in Count 2. And I stand here to implore you, as I plead Dr. Karadzic's case and for his life, to ask me any and all questions you have so I can clear out the smoke that the Prosecution has created to mask the weakness of its case on this count. Let's start with something that's not in dispute. Not a single witness has testified that Radovan Karadzic planned, ordered, or was even informed about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica. Think about that. And you have to ask yourselves why. Maybe one reason is that it simply isn't true. Radovan Karadzic never planned, ordered, or was even informed about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica. Despite having unprecedented access to thousands of intercepted, private conversations, thousands of written communications of the Republika Srpska military, police, and political organs, and hundreds of speeches and interviews of Dr. Karadzic, there is not a single piece of evidence that Dr. Karadzic planned, ordered, or even was informed about the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica. Srebrenica is the most well-documented crime in any war crimes tribunal since Nuremberg. You can follow the events of July 1995 minute by minute, place by place, through intercepts, satellite imagery, written reports, orders, and log-book entries. Yet there's not a single piece of evidence that shows that Dr. Karadzic planned or ordered the execution of prisoners from Srebrenica or that he even knew that they would be, were being, or had been executed. The Prosecution's case relies solely on inference. Dr. Karadzic was the president of Republika Srpska and Commander-in-Chief of the Bosnian army. He was closely following the Srebrenica events and he issued orders during those events to the army, to the police, and to the civilian authorities of Srebrenica. Therefore, he must have planned and ordered the execution which followed. But we submit to you that that is not the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from this evidence. Another more reasonable inference is that Dr. Karadzic never planned or ordered those executions and that, in fact, they were concealed from him and that he is not guilty of genocide. The Appeals Chamber has repeatedly held that when the Prosecution relies upon proof of the state of mind of an accused by inference, that inference must be the only reasonable inference available on the evidence. And they said that the benefit of the doubt must always go to the accused. The Defence case doesn't rely on inference. We brought everybody who could possibly speak to Dr. Karadzic's actions and knowledge of the Srebrenica events to come and testify at this trial. People who worked for him in his office, held meetings with him, and even those convicted of participating in the crimes themselves were brought to this courtroom, sometimes willingly, sometimes kicking and screaming by subpoena. But to a man, they testified that Dr. Karadzic was not informed of those executions and played no role in their commission. The scales of justice on this issue are unbalanced. The Prosecutor's case is supported solely by inference. The Defence case is supported by hard evidence. Now, I'm sorry to have to do this orally in such detail, but since we didn't have the right to file a written reply to the Prosecutor's final brief, let me take some minutes to deconstruct, brick by brick, the Prosecution's house of inferences that comprises its case for genocide against Dr. Karadzic in connection with Srebrenica. Fact: On the 9th of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now, you can please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Fact: On the 9th of July, 1995, Dr. Karadzic ordered the VRS to take the town of Srebrenica and ordered them to offer maximum protection and safety to the civilian population and to treat the civilian members of the population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions. The Prosecution's inference is that this order facilitated the plan to execute the men of Srebrenica and was part of repeated efforts to cloak written orders implementing illegal objectives with simulated adherence to international law. We submit that another reasonable inference is that the order meant what it said, that Dr. Karadzic had no intention that civilians or prisoners be mistreated, let alone murdered. Fact: In the late evening of 11 July, Dr. Karadzic issued an order appointing Miroslav Deronjic civilian commissioner. His order provided that the commissioner shall ensure that all civilian and military organs treat all citizens who participated in combat against the Army of Republika Srpska as prisoners of war and ensure that the civilian population can freely choose where they will live or move to. Fact: At the same time, Dr. Karadzic issued an order for the establishment of a public security station in Srebrenica. His order provided that all citizens who participated in combat activities against the Serb army will be treated as prisoners of war and in accordance with the law and with international conventions. Others will be free to choose their place of residence or place of emigration. The Prosecution wants you to infer that this was another simulation of adherence to law that belied Karadzic's true intent that the men from Srebrenica be executed. We say there's another reasonable inference, that the order meant what it said, that Dr. Karadzic had no intention that civilians or prisoners be mistreated, let alone murdered. Fact: On the evening of 11 July 1995, Dr. Karadzic issued an order concerning the passage of humanitarian convoys through the territory of Republika Srpska. That's P5183 and I ask you to study that. The aim stated in the order was to eliminate problems in the passage of UN convoys. The Prosecution would like you to infer that this order became a means by which Karadzic controlled access to the enclave by international organisations, including UNHCR and ICRC, allowing the murder operation to proceed unchecked. We say that another reasonable inference is clear that the purpose of the order was to improve the passage of convoys, not to hinder them, as evidenced by the reference to the danger of international intervention because of the need to get humanitarian aid to affected civilians and the threat of punishment for anyone obstructing the convoys. The order loosened restrictions by prohibiting inspections and providing an escort between the border and the front line. Having taken the drastic action of overrunning a UN safe area, Dr. Karadzic wanted to make sure that there were no reasons for NATO to use force on the grounds that humanitarian aid could not reach the affected people. Fact: Dr. Karadzic met with Deputy Minister of Interior Tomo Kovac from 1550 to 1610 on the 13th of July and again on 14 July from 2245 to 2310. The Prosecution inference is that Karadzic met with Kovac on the 13th of July, sent him to arrange the logistics of the murder operation with General Mladic, and then Kovac reported back to him on the 14th of July. We say that another reasonable inference is that Kovac never received instructions from Dr. Karadzic concerning the murder of Muslim prisoners and never informed Dr. Karadzic of any executions. And we point out that there is no written order or intercepted communication indicating that Kovac had anything to do with arranging the logistics of the murder operation. Kovac's testimony was unequivocal that he had not participated in the murder operation nor discussed any killings with Dr. Karadzic. If Kovac was supposed to arrange the logistics of the murder operation with Mladic, how does that explain his order on the 14th of July, that the police were to have nothing to do with the prisoners? And we have testimony of that not only from Kovac but from Borovcanin and from Mane Djuric. Borovcanin is paragraph 41 of his amalgamated statement at D3659; and Mane Djuric's testimony is at page 35043 and 44 of the transcript. But most important, what about that intercepted call between Beara and Krstic on the morning of the 15th of July, P5074, when Colonel Beara complained that MUP "won't do anything." Fact: Dr. Karadzic spoke with Miroslav Deronjic on 13 July at 2010. Deronjic informed him that they had 2.000 and that there would be more during the night. Dr. Karadzic said that "all goods must be placed in the warehouses by 12.00 tomorrow - not in warehouses there but somewhere else." Deronjic said he understood. The Prosecution's inference that they would like you to draw is that Karadzic's phone call with Deronjic, telling him that the prisoners had to be placed somewhere else referred to Zvornik. We think there's another reasonable inference, that Dr. Karadzic was referring to Batkovici prison which was the normal place for prisoners to be taken. How could Deronjic possibly understand from this conversation that prisoners were to be sent to Zvornik? It's a more reasonable inference that if Dr. Karadzic was referring to any specific location at all, he was referring to Batkovici prison, a place to which the ICRC had regular access. And Milenko Todorovic testified that they received instructions at one point to prepare Batkovici prison to receive prisoners from Srebrenica. You can find that at D4124 at pages 12934, 38, 39, and 41. The use of code on unsecured lines when referring to the location of prisoners was likewise not nefarious, but so that the enemy would not know where they were being held and mount a rescue operation, in our submission. Fact: On 14 July, Dr. Karadzic issued a decision proclaiming a state of war in Srebrenica-Skelani municipality. The decision indicates that the aim of proclaiming a state of war is to enable the full engagement of human and material resources in the defence of the republic and final victory over the enemy. It further provided that the armed forces and government organs shall observe the provisions of international law and international conventions regulating the conduct of a state during a state of war. The Prosecution wants you to infer that Karadzic issued this decision to give Deronjic extraordinary powers and to facilitate the use of civilian personnel and equipment for the murder and burial operations, and they claim that the column no longer posed such a threat to Srebrenica and Skelani so as to justify this decision. We say that another reasonable inference is the aim of the decision was as it is stated, to mobilise resources to defend the municipality. Exhibit P2803 at line 340, the republic communications centre log, indicates that this decision was issued at 11.55 a.m. on the 14th of July. On the morning of the 14th of July, the chaos in the woods around Srebrenica still existed and the VRS reported that its units were scouring the terrain around Srebrenica. That's the daily combat report received early that morning, P4464 at page 3. Robert Djurdjevic testified that when he met with President Karadzic in the afternoon of the 14th of July, the army was reporting that there was a lot of fighting between Konjevic Polje and Kasaba. This had nothing to do with murders and burials. If Dr. Karadzic had indeed ordered the transport of the prisoners to Zvornik on the evening of the 13th of July to kill them, as the Prosecution claims, and wanted to conceal murders and burials, the order would have included Zvornik municipality. Fact: On the 16th -- and this deals with the corridor, the opening of the corridor. On the 16th of July at 1529, someone from the VRS Main Staff called the duty officer of the Drina Corps and said: "I have to get permission from the main boss, from the main head of state," and he asked him to "have Vinko tell you what happened and send it right away." Fact: On 1615 of the same day, less than an hour later, the VRS Main Staff duty officer informed General Mladic that the president had called a short while ago and said that he had been informed by Karisik that Pandurevic arranged passage for the Muslims over to that territory. And those are Exhibits P5076 and D2002. The Prosecution's inference is that Karadzic's call to the VRS about opening a corridor reveal that he was concerned about Muslims getting away, while the killing and burial operations in Zvornik were proceeding as planned. And yesterday they told us that the Main Staff had to get permission because the opening of a corridor was a variation from the plan to kill all the Muslims of Srebrenica. We think that another reasonable inference from these conversations was that Dr. Karadzic was in favour of opening the corridor. His inquiry was prompted by a call from Karisik. As you've heard from a protected witness - and you can find this at P4563, page 3 - Dragomir Vasic, Karisik's subordinate, was in favour of opening the corridor. Karisik himself was personally engaged in trying to get the captured policemen returned safely across the line. His call to Karadzic would likely have been to encourage him to support Pandurevic's opening of the corridor. Karadzic spoke favourably about opening the corridor during his 17 July interview with David Frost. You saw that yesterday. And that's P5235, pages 2 and 3 of the transcript. President Karadzic's discussion about opening the corridor at the 6th August 1995 Assembly session was made in the context of trying to fire General Mladic. He complained about combat tactics, spending time in Zepa without leaving sufficient troops to battle the forces from Srebrenica and taking many losses of life as a result. And that's P1412 at page 17. But even if President Karadzic was opposed to opening of the corridor from the beginning, so what? The Prosecution has conceded that the column was a legitimate military target and could be attacked. There's nothing genocidal in inflicting as many losses on combatants as possible. This had nothing to do with the fate of the prisoners. Just another straw that the Prosecution is grasping at. Fact: As reported by the Bratunac Brigade on 18 July, Dr. Karadzic had pardoned all the local staff who worked for UNPROFOR and they were not detained. The Prosecution's inference is that without Karadzic's amnesty, the UN local staff would have been killed and Karadzic's control over the murder operation was such that he had the power of life or death over the Muslim men and boys of Srebrenica. We think another reasonable inference is that Karadzic did not favour or condone any killings and did not have the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim group. This is an example that no good deed goes unpunished in the eyes of the Prosecution. Fact: The ICRC gained access to Batkovici camp on the 26th of July and the Srebrenica-Bratunac area on the 27th of July. And this is P2284, the UN report on Srebrenica at paragraph 409. The Prosecution wants you to infer that Karadzic either ignored or rejected requests by the UN or international organisations for access to the Srebrenica and Bratunac areas. Another reasonable inference is that the first letter requesting such access from Mr. Mazowiecki was sent to Dr. Karadzic on the 25th of July - that's P6396 - and they got access the next day. Fact: On the 2nd of August, Beara and Stevo from the Main Staff discussed getting the Muslims who were detained in Srebrenica back to Republika Srpska. Stevo said that the ICRC was registering them and Beara said: "We had no plans to kill them, just exchange them ... you think it would be no good if Karadzic or someone else," and then it trailed off. This is P4972 at page 4. The Prosecution's inference is that Karadzic approved efforts to retrieve Muslims from Syria to make up for a lack of prisoners to exchange and they say Beara referred to Karadzic in this conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you meant Serbia, not Syria.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, if I said "Syria," I'm mistaken. I'm sorry about that. We say that another reasonable inference is that there is no evidence that Karadzic had anything to do with retrieving Muslims from Serbia or had any knowledge of a shortage of prisoners from Srebrenica. Beara may well have been saying that it would be no good if Karadzic agreed to exchanges and then the lack of prisoners from Srebrenica became known. We think that this shows that Karadzic had no knowledge that the prisoners would be executed or had been executed. And there were reasons for people in the VRS to have concealed executions from President Karadzic. He had held them back from taking Srebrenica in 1993, and he had insisted that they withdraw from Mount Igman in August of 1993 in the sharpest of terms, as you've heard from those intercepts in that period. And he held them back from taking Gorazde in April 1994. He had issued dozens of orders, insisting that they comply with international law. They knew he would never approve of executing prisoners and that he would view such a thing as treason against Republika Srpska, which he does. Fact: On the 12th of August, 1995, the Republika Srpska Commission for Exchange of Prisoners reported that a large number of Muslim soldiers had now been captured across Republika Srpska and proposed a one-for-one exchange, and this is Exhibit P4975. They said that the Muslims detained in Batkovici could be freed in exchange for 170 Serbs held prisoner in the Tuzla area. They proposed to get Serbs held captive in Sarajevo by exchanging even more Muslim prisoners "captured during the activities of liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa." And finally, they proposed to get Serbs held in the Zenica area by exchanging Muslims held by the 1st Krajina Corps, supplemented by prisoners from other areas of Republika Srpska. And I ask you to look at that document carefully. The Prosecution's inference is that Karadzic received a report from the state commission, which said that there were no more than a few hundred Muslim men from Srebrenica at Batkovici camp. But we say that the other reasonable inference to be drawn from this evidence is that there were a large number of Muslim prisoners available for exchange. There was nothing in this report that would lead Dr. Karadzic to believe that there was a shortage of prisoners from Srebrenica; quite the contrary. And that's it. That's the Prosecution's case against Dr. Karadzic for Srebrenica. And as thin as it is to begin with, it simply falls apart when separating fact from inference and when determining whether the inferences that the Prosecution seeks to draw are the only reasonable inferences from the evidence. Taken individually and collectively, the Prosecution's case is insufficient to establish beyond a reasonable doubt that Dr. Karadzic was part of a joint criminal enterprise to eliminate the men of Srebrenica or even had knowledge of their execution. Contrast that with the Defence case. You know how difficult it is to prove a negative, yet 28 witnesses testified that Dr. Karadzic was not informed of the Srebrenica executions. Those witnesses included high-ranking officials in the army, the police, the secret services, and the Assembly. They included a Canadian intelligence officer, Witness KW554, who went looking through intelligence reports to see what involvement Dr. Karadzic had in the executions and found that he had none. As you know from litigation before this Chamber, Dr. Karadzic, at his own initiative, requested from a number of countries, including the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Germany, and Canada, any evidence they had reflecting his knowledge of the executions at Srebrenica. He did that because he knew the truth, that he had no knowledge of those executions. And his position is confirmed by the fact that not a single country produced even a scrap of evidence showing that Dr. Karadzic had knowledge of the executions, much less planned or ordered them. If Dr. Karadzic were truly guilty of the Srebrenica killings, you would have heard something more than what the Prosecution has presented in five years of trial, and you certainly would not have heard the massive evidence presented by the Defence on this issue. The Prosecution has never explained why, if Dr. Karadzic had planned, ordered, or even had knowledge of the Srebrenica executions, he went out of his way to take credit for the Srebrenica operation, both on national television on the 4th of August, when he said General Krstic had planned the Srebrenica operation in front of him, and at the Assembly on the 16th of October, 1995, when he had said that he personally supervised the plan and personally ordered General Krstic to take Srebrenica. A lot of bad things have been said about Dr. Karadzic, but nobody ever said that he's stupid. But even if you somehow believe that Dr. Karadzic had knowledge that the men of Srebrenica were executed, you must still find him not guilty of genocide because genocide requires something more, that general -- that Dr. Karadzic had the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslims as such. And as we saw with Count 1, there is no evidence that Dr. Karadzic had that intent, not in 1992, not in 1995. For aiding and abetting genocide, Dr. Karadzic would have to have known of the genocidal intent of others, yet the evidence that has been found in other cases at this Tribunal to support a finding that genocide was committed at Srebrenica was unknown to Dr. Karadzic. In the Krstic case, the Trial Chamber found that the fact that the VRS sought to kill every Muslim man it could find, civilian or military, was indicative of an intent to destroy the group. There is no evidence from which it can be inferred that President Karadzic knew that the VRS had sought to kill every man from Srebrenica. In fact, he was informed that the VRS had opened a corridor so that men from Srebrenica could proceed to Muslim territory, and he himself ordered the local Muslim UN staff from Srebrenica to be allowed to leave. The Krstic Trial Chamber also based its finding of an intent to destroy on the concealment of the bodies and the prevention of proper burials for those who were killed. There's no evidence of any of this being brought to President Karadzic's attention. The Appeals Chamber found that General Krstic's knowledge of genocide could not be inferred from his contacts with General Mladic, which were substantial; his participation in the Hotel Fontana meeting; his presence in Potocari; his order to secure the road where men were removed from buses; and the participation of members of the Drina Corps in the executions. President Karadzic did not have any of these contacts in Srebrenica and therefore had even less reason to know of the genocidal intent of some VRS officers, if that intent existed. In the Blagojevic case, the Trial Chamber inferred that Blagojevic knew of the genocidal intent of those participating in the executions, primarily from his knowledge of the transfer of women and children, the executions in Bratunac town, and that his forces were trying to capture Muslim men and prevent them from reaching Muslim territory. But the Appeals Chamber reversed this finding, concluding that without knowledge of the mass killings, Blagojevic did not have knowledge of the perpetrators' genocidal intent. President Karadzic had even less information than Colonel Blagojevic, therefore the Blagojevic case supports a finding that the evidence is insufficient to infer knowledge of genocide by President Karadzic. In the Popovic case, the Trial Chamber found that despite commander Vinko Pandurevic's direct knowledge of the murder operation, there was no evidence that he knew of the key features of the operation indicating genocidal intent, the indiscriminate separations in Potocari, the vigorous pursuit of every last Muslim male along the Bratunac-Konjevic Polje road, the large component of civilians amongst the prisoners, the details of the executions, or the systematic nature of the operation. Likewise, President Karadzic did not know Colonel Beara or Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, nor did he have any contact with them. None of the information he received indicated that there had been any indiscriminate separations in Potocari, vigorous pursuit of every last Muslim male, or failure to distinguish between civilians and soldiers. Therefore, he had no reason to know of any of the facts indicating that the killings had been perpetrated with genocidal intent. The Popovic Trial Chamber also found that Ljubomir Borovcanin had no reason to know of the genocidal intent with which the crimes were committed, despite his being on the scene and having actual knowledge of the Kravica warehouse killings, and acquitted him of genocide. The information brought to President Karadzic's attention after the fact was not as encompassing or specific as that possessed by Borovcanin; therefore he too must be acquitted of genocide even if you find that he had some information about murders. Let me once again make it clear that unspeakable crimes were committed after the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995. Thousands of Bosnian Muslim prisoners were executed and the victims of those crimes never had any chance for justice. They were summarily executed by the likes of Franz Kos and Drazen Erdemovic, without a lawyer, without a trial, and without a verdict. Dr. Karadzic has had a Defence team, a five-year trial, and will have a verdict from three learned international Judges. That is a testament to the humanity of mankind and I'm proud to have been part of these proceedings. This trial has already established the principle that as a society, no matter how heinous the crime, we value justice over barbarity. But just as it was a grave injustice to condemn the victims of Srebrenica, it would be a grave injustice to condemn Dr. Karadzic for crimes he did not commit, and genocide is one of those crimes. Therefore, I ask you to find Dr. Karadzic not guilty on Count 2. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. We'll have a break for an hour and resume -- a break for 20 minutes and we'll continue at 10.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all. As the Defence, I feel handicapped after the plea made by Mr. Robinson. I shall appear even more as an amateur, but of course I shall be adducing the facts and you will appreciate the lack of form. I should like to turn to what the Prosecutor is saying about Sarajevo in its final brief as having been established in Sarajevo. The Prosecution bases its case about Sarajevo on the theory that there existed a Serbian policy of producing terror, intimidating the citizens of Sarajevo, and it infers such conclusions from a number of sources, from several reporters, and from an insider. The first and most often quoted sources are international observers, journalists, UNPROFOR members, and members of other organisations. The second source are Muslim investigators of the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina who investigated the various incidents. And the third source are several witnesses who lived in Sarajevo at that time. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: The first three sources, international observers, Muslim investigators, and the inhabitants of Sarajevo, during the trial and cross-examination have proven to be exceptionally unreliable. Sometimes so into their obvious partiality and their effort to accommodate the expectations of the Prosecution and at other times because of their obvious ignorance and lack of knowledge of the situation. And all these three sources, globally speaking, contested the very existence of units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the existence of heavy weaponry of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the city itself or the strength and numbers of those forces. Representing the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had 80.000 combatants of whom about 40- or 50.000, the 12th Division, which was always in the city, and the rest are on the outer ring is something inconsequential and negligible and unimportant. This made it possible for the Prosecution to create the impression that there was no war, as if there were no army there, as if war had not been declared on Serbs, and as if the Serbs had come from somewhere and laid siege to Sarajevo with forces that had nothing to do whatsoever with Sarajevo; whereas it was quite simple and easy to establish that that was not the case, that both the inhabitants of Sarajevo, everybody, was just guarding their own neighbourhoods, their own settlements, whereas -- and the Serbs did not have any ambitions of taking the city, taking the Muslim section of the city. And the Muslims did have that ambition, to capture the Serbian part of the city. And when one reads or hears what the Prosecution holds against the Serbs -- charges the Serbs with in terms of their conduct surrounding Sarajevo, that is more like an ideological and political [indiscernible]: Shame on you, you opened fire, you were shooting while neglecting the laws of war, the legitimate and customs of war, the legitimate rights of peoples, creating an impression that everything was just one-sided. One was unmotivated and everything was unjustified. International representatives invoked -- the statements of which the Prosecution invokes, actually ventured to characterised the Serbian strategy, plans, and other confidential information which they could not even dream of. They were nowhere near the decision-making of the Army of Republika Srpska or the local or state and municipal organs of Republika Srpska. Nowhere where decisions were made were they present or knew anything about it, but they drew their superficial conclusions mainly on the basis of some superficial observation of the battle-front in Sarajevo, very limited views with distorted -- and they -- conclusions. And they sat in their shelters and wherever they were, their positions, receiving information from their Muslim interpreters and in other ways. As a rule, they never saw the heavy weaponry in Sarajevo. As a rule, they never registered the thousands of shells which the units of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina fired from the city, targeting the Serbian section of the city. As a rule, they observed everything which was done from hill to hill, across Sarajevo valley. That was always the Serb fire, although not a single foot was there where there was only a Serbian soldier without having a Croat or a Muslim Croat opposite him, trench opposite trench. Everything which came from the hill was fired by the Serbs, although a number of salient features which are near, the elevations which are near to Sarajevo were held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serbs held those which were farther away. They would just register fire in response which the Serbs were firing to respond, and they characterised it as they saw fit. You will see one witness said: I know, I concluded that it was random fire because it was not concentrated fire, it was just one or two shells. Another witness again said: I know that the purpose was to terrorise because the fire was concentrated. However, we have even as many as two daily reports of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the Main Staff, these are all coded documents, confidential, secret documents, in which no one from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps would actually dare lie to the Main Staff. And certainly not intend any of its content for any propaganda purposes. The question of the response of the conduct in firing, the expenditure of ammunition lists in the reports of the SRK, begs possible just a single and one conclusion which is that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps comported itself with maximum degree of responsibility up to the level, the limits of sustainability of endurance and refrain from responding. Here we have heard that there was a contradiction in the testimony and documents of General Milosevic. Allegedly he said that these were uncontrolled elements and that must have been the SRK. If they were uncontrolled elements, that just could not have been the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. It simply was not, is not the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Thus, international observers simply did not know at a single point in time the disposition of forces of the respective forces in Sarajevo and their respective strengths, their numbers, their fire-power. They never counted the shells that fell on Serbian territory. They never observed or noticed who started first, but they did, in fact. And Harland says that in a certain period, the Muslims violated the truce, the cease-fire agreement 318 times. If someone of them was asked, like Mr. Doyle, if they knew where the disposition was of the Muslim forces, how did they know who opened fire. He said: I don't know, I didn't know, it was not my obligation to know where the respective armies were because his role was a different, diplomatic one. Then he should not have been asked about these matters. Someone else, in fact, should have been asked about that. To briefly touch upon the Muslim investigators and policemen as the second source of information and of documents for the Prosecution case in respect of the Sarajevo segment. In addition to their purported lack of information of the Muslim investigators and policemen about the strength and the disposition of the 1st Corps, their own army, in Sarajevo, during the investigation they demonstrated exceptional lack of objectivity and lack of professionalism in their work when they conducted on-site investigations of alleged incidents. The witnesses avoided direct and compromising questions and they -- the excuse was that this was not within their remit, evidence was distorted. The maps of Sarajevo were shown upside down and they were turned. The azimuth, the north direction would be changed by 90 degrees in order to show that a specific projectile had been fired from the Serbian side. We remember the sniping incidents in Nehru Street where a girl, a young woman was killed through a darkened window at night and the investigator said: We did not do the deflection according to the horizontal plane, but it was quite obvious by the vertical plane that the bullet actually went up by 70 centimetres from 2.5 metres. So the upward trajectory was easy to determine, and on that basis they determined that this was fired by the Serbs. Namely, these investigators according -- in their own admission, actually, did not work the way they worked in peace time. They did not prepare and conduct their investigations and complete the documentation as they would have done otherwise. I must have spoken very quickly because the transcript does not reflect my words faithfully. So lines 17 and on. This girl was shot but she was not visible. It was night and the window was shut. The blinds were down. She was not visible. This bullet which hit her had an upwards trajectory, and we know that an upward trajectory by vertical -- along the vertical line we do know but not along the horizontal plane. The deflection should have been along the horizontal plane, if it had been fired from the Serbian side, at least 45 degrees or more because the Serbian positions were obliquely positioned vis-à-vis that window. One investigates by coming to that window and looking at the Serbian positions and just saying that is where the bullet came from. The witnesses who were inhabitants of Sarajevo, identically as other groups of prosecutorial witnesses, alleged that they did not know anything about the hundreds and thousands of soldiers that passed by them daily going to their shifts, conducting manoeuvres, hauling weapons, shooting. They did not know, they did not see them shooting from the skyscrapers, from the hospitals, museums, schools. They did not see 275 staffs of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in this very narrow urban core strip of Sarajevo. So many brigades, battalions, companies. How many can there be that they have 275 staffs and command posts? And they created the impression and actually testified as if it had only been a unilateral barbarian assault of the Serbs, of the Serbian army, which was composed of their fellow citizens, without any reason, without any cause. This is how the international representatives comported themselves. General Michael Rose, on page 7308, line 2 -- 23 and page 7309, confirmed that the identification of the firing point, the position from which the mortar is fired was very imprecise, a very imprecise science, generally speaking, in a very large majority of cases, and that different views, different possibilities, have to be taken into consideration for any further investigation to be conducted. General Rose testified in the Karadzic case on transcript page 7335, saying that Ganic organised his secret police to open sniper fire at a tram. I'm going to read this out in English: [In English] "His sniper units sniped so that the angle of the shot matched the direction from the Serb lines." [Interpretation] The witness says that UNPROFOR did not have its own intelligence service and an information-gathering service and therefore they did not carry out investigations. Also, he said that they received reports from Sector South of UNPROFOR, and he confirms that it is his conviction that at that time Ganic organised his secret police and sniped at the tram. As for this situation, every incident that is ascribed to the Serb army is something that the Prosecution has to prove. It's not the Defence that has to prove whose sniper shooter that was. It is the Prosecution that has to prove what happened, if there is such a possibility; and if this possibility was established, that that is what they were doing. And we heard that from other witnesses too that the Seve, larks, and others did that. General Rose, in response to the question put by this Defence, answered that the only way in which it can be established with certainty what the source of mortar fire was was a radar and there wasn't one there at the time. The witness said that on page 3755 to 76. General Rose rejected all allegations that the United Nations allowed the Muslim army to use their positions in order to fire at the Serbs. However, there is an UNPROFOR document of the 8th of November, 1994, that is D696, registers the fact that the Muslim forces were observed as they used or abused UN insignia, helmets, white vehicles, in order to create an impression -- or, rather, to operate more easily and to pass off as the UN. This testimony is on page 7464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you give us again the reference of General Rose testifying that Ganic's -- in relation to Ganic's sniping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, with pleasure. The reference I have is numbers 2 and 3, so that is the testimony in the Karadzic case, page 7335, lines 6 through 19; and page 7335, line 24; and on page -36 to line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I have in front of me is this, it is your question saying: "Do you remember that Ejub Ganic had organised secret police that sniped the trams in Sarajevo and all those incidents were supposed to be assigned to the Serbian side, the Serbs were to be blamed for all those?" That was your question. And I have his answer which says: "Well, as I explained before, we had no intelligence-gathering capability, so I wouldn't be -- have been at the time able to confirm or deny such an allegation and I certainly can't do so today." Do you have more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll check that until the break, but we are convinced that it was confirmed by General Rose, that he confirmed this about the tricks that we asked him about. Maybe he didn't know at that point in time, but later on he learned about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecutor Gustafson said that General Rose did not confirm, as we said in our paragraph 2313 of our final brief, that UNPROFOR smuggled weapons for the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In that paragraph we relied on document D688, page 4, which was shown to Rose on page 7425 and 26. And we didn't even say that it was Rose who said that; however, we proved to him and to the Prosecution that UNPROFOR, the UNHCR, and the other so-called humanitarian organisations smuggled - of course it was individuals but that doesn't change the fact - smuggled weapons and in other ways helped the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were therefore partial and they took part in the conflict in that way. This is also proven in other paragraphs of our final brief. For example, paragraph 1329, 2335, 2986, and the documents that our final brief relies on, that is, D2168, D2170, D3575, D3302, D3303, D2122, D2123, D3307, D3286, D2123, D3308, D4145 on page 3, D2336, D2512, D2513, D2605, D2606. These are but a few examples; to be more specific, 18 examples of different cases during the war that show that what General Rose said was not accurate. He either did not know about it or he could not allow himself to say the truth. So this document was put to the witness, a document that shows that the Muslim soldiers were masked in UNPROFOR uniforms, that they used UNPROFOR insignia, that they painted their vehicles white, and they wore UNPROFOR helmets. The testimony of General Rose -- I mean what I said about them asking, that was on page 7466 from line 21 to 7466 line 13. The Bosnian government, it says there in the documents, would stop that when protests were lodged. General Rose claimed that UNPROFOR did not know whether there were any violations of the arms embargo in Bosnia-Herzegovina because they did not have an intelligence service. 15 years after that, it was clear that there was an active programme of violating the arms embargo and this was done by various countries throughout the world. And General Rose confirmed that on page 7476, lines 3 to 15. In response to a question put by the Defence, the witness confirmed that the Western countries had a total lack of understanding of the nature of the conflict, also that they had a strategy of confusion in terms of having the situation resolved. That is on pages 7322, lines 16 through 19. The Trial Chamber can draw its own conclusions as to what the consequences are for the warring parties, especially the Serb side, and how important the testimony of officials from these countries is, these countries that did not have enough knowledge or enough understanding, that did not understand the nature of the conflict sufficiently. In response to Karadzic's question, the witness, General Rose, stated that his view of UNMOs, UN Military Observers, whose reports or testimony are a significant stronghold of the Prosecution case against Karadzic and the generals and soldiers of the Serb army, on page 7294 from line 5 to 19, he confirmed that they did not have the necessary experience to view and understand the fighting from a tactical point of view. Their reports were often unreliable and they had a direct line of communication with New York. And they could be susceptible to propaganda of international institutions and the international media. His own interview was shown to Rose in which he said that he believed that Ganic had organised his secret police to snipe at trams. He stated that on page T ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That interview was shown to General Rose, and 7335 is the page where this is referred to and the interview was 1D2475. It hadn't been admitted but General Rose did not deny giving that interview. Your Excellency, that is an answer to your question as to what the reference pertains to, the reference concerning Ganic and his snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to Dr. Karadzic's question, the witness, General Rose, said that it could not be established beyond any doubt or with precision from where the sniper shots had come because proper investigations were not carried out and it was impossible to establish beyond a reasonable doubt who it was that was shooting. Francis Roy Thomas, yet another representative of the UN force, on page 6832, confirmed that it was impossible to establish from where a shell arrived in Markale on the 5th of February, 1994. D634 describes the activity of the 101st Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, there is another description that near that platoon there were a few other platoons, mortar platoons, then the 2nd Viteska Motorised Brigade. Mr. Thomas, Francis Roy Thomas, spoke about that on page 6909. And a brigade artillery group of the 5th Motorised Brigade existed as well; 6910 is the page where he refers to that, and that is also recorded in document D634. However, Mr. Thomas was not aware of the kind of fire that the 102nd Motorised Brigade could have used; 6912 is the page reference, again in relation to the same document, D634. The 2nd Motorised Brigade was around the PTT building where the UN headquarters was and it was visible to one and all. Each and every piece of weaponry could be seen as well. Mr. Thomas testified on page 6835, stating that mortar projectiles at that time in Sarajevo could have been fired from any side. And then he claims that any larger calibre would have to be fired from the Serb side allegedly because the Muslims did not have large calibres in town. First of all, in town the Muslims did indeed have large calibres and that can be seen in document D634. Secondly, the Muslim army could reach the Serb part of Sarajevo from other positions as well by firing large calibres from Igman and from the positions of the 16th Division, on the outer ring around Sarajevo, the outer confrontation line. Thomas identified the victims of the incidents that were shown to him in morgues and medical institutions. He was not able to differentiate among people who were killed on the front line and people who died in other ways, and he had no sources that would have enabled him to do so. We will direct the Chamber to a document that shows how many soldiers were killed in Sarajevo. That is -- first of all, concerning the medical institutions and mortuaries, that was said on page 6860. And when he said that he was not able to differentiate between people who died in different ways, that was on page 6861. Using the services of regular military observers they established a cause of death. He said that on page 6861. The military observers of the United Nations made their judgements and conclusions interpreting from the context. They erred and their errors were in the differentiation between combatants and civilians. They were not able to distinguish even among the living people who was a soldier and who was a civilian, that's on page 6863. His testimony, therefore, is flawed and lacks weight, not because it was intentional but because his knowledge was limited. Another witness described random, indiscriminate fire from large-calibre weapons as fire that was not concentrated on a particular zone with the intent of targeting a particular military objective. That witness was Richard Mole. All this is to be found on page 5818 and 5819, lines 1 to 19; and on the previous page it was lines 20 to 25. The fire was indirect, imprecise, and as such it was not concentrated from that type of weapon and it was impossible to determine a pattern of targeting so this fire can be qualified as indiscriminate, but we've heard testimony of commanders from Ozrenska Street and documents where they report to the corps command, saying: We are under fire, we are suffering great losses, but we then fired a shell to shut them down. Every military prosecutor and every military judge knows how artillery is used. In this Office of the Prosecutor, I have not seen any person of that profile. In these circumstances, fire can be used. General Karavelic said - and I thought he would come to testify - said that the SRK used artillery fire just as the 1st Corps of the BiH. To neutralise a firing position, you can use artillery to shut down, to destroy, to harass a firing position of the enemy. It all depends on whether the fire is proportionate. We will equally see that another witness, cited by Ms. Gustafson, said that he could recognise random fire intended to terrorise by the fact that it was concentrated, which is completely contrary to what Mole says. So we see there are two criteria for determining wrong use of artillery by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. Such indirect conclusions were used by the Prosecution to contend that there had been indiscriminate and terrorising artillery fire against the city. Maybe for ordinary purposes this can be done, but in every judicial system, including in our country, higher standards would apply. The Defence has also shown that the Muslims targeted their own section of the city and they put it to the witness, Mole, and Mole responded that the observers felt that could have been the case but they did not have enough evidence. And he says on page 5886, lines 3 through 11, that they did not have the capability to carry out a satisfactory forensic investigation. Concerning the Muslims, the Prosecution does not even require a satisfactory forensic investigation, but when they deal with chitchat on the telephone that can be used against the Serbs, that is useful and it is used. Ms. Gustafson contended there was no evidence in the reports of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina fired at their own civilians. Maybe the Defence referred to the wrong documents, but the following documents speak to this. D2796 states: "The Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina is firing with RPGs and infantry weapons from positions above Breka at Bascarsija and their own positions with the intention of blaming the Serbs." In document 2797 -- all these are D documents, D2797 and D2796. In a report of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to the higher command, it is said that the BH army is opening artillery fire [as interpreted] at the city and the UN command in order to ascribe that fire to the Serbs. I said "machine-gun fire." It was wrongly recorded as "artillery fire." This report refers to machine-gun fire. In addition, the Prosecution did not mention a word about KW586, who was part of the presidential security detail, and he heard and saw with his own eyes when Izetbegovic and his leadership were making plans for massacres of their own population, as described in our final brief paragraph 1977 and 29 -- sorry, 2099. And there is evidence of that and this evidence was available to the Prosecution. To continue with Lieutenant-Colonel Mole, on page 5886 he confirmed his statement from 1997 when he said that the Muslim side was using Sarajevo in order to maintain their victim status. On page 5887 he confirmed that in cross-examination. Officer Banbury, in his testimony in the Galic case, shared the same views and that was confirmed on page 5886, lines 18 through 25. There were common areas where Muslims could assemble, such as market-places or lines or queues for humanitarian aid were a frequent target that the Muslims used to fire at their own people. That was said on page 5889, lines 1 through 15. Lieutenant-Colonel Mole in his evidence said he believed that Muslims gained advantage by causing suffering in Sarajevo which won them sympathy from others and that is why they kept their own civilians locked in Sarajevo. It was for that purpose. He said that on page 5889 from line 17 through 22. He also confirmed on page 5890 that there were not enough groups of UNMOs to investigate all the shells, all possible fire, all incidents in that area, nor was it their mission to judge what was proper and what was not around the confrontation line. That's on page 5852. Lieutenant-Colonel Mole confirmed that they did not conduct investigations in the police sense of the word nor did they investigate responsibility for individual incidents. That was because cease-fires never held and it was very difficult under the circumstances of such military activity to establish anything. So their reports cannot be used as evidence in a criminal trial. His testimony is to be found on page 5852. It's confirmed, thus, that they did not conduct investigations that would be usable in a criminal trial and they did not investigate responsibility for particular incidents of fire. There were things that Lieutenant-Colonel Mole heard about only and things that never found their way into UNMO reports. He confirmed that on page 5884. He says on page 5895 and 5896 that it was impossible to record all activity of heavy weapons. It was irrelevant, he says, and useless to try to concentrate on a particular incident such as targeting of UN vehicles or to determine the origin of fire. And the material provided by military observers are a source of many charges concerning Sarajevo. As for observation posts, their number was limited by the number of officers and the UNMOs complain they did not have enough personnel, that's on page 5810. In a certain number of daily entries, there were large differences between the number of shells incoming and outgoing from Sarajevo on one hand and the number of outgoing shells from Sarajevo falling on the Serbian side on the other. That was on page 5815. In cross-examination, Lieutenant-Colonel Mole confirmed that they were not in a position to place their observers on Mount Igman, and the imprecision and inaccuracy in recording the number of shells is due partly to the fact that there was no observation of outgoing fire from Mount Igman. Lieutenant-Colonel Mole admitted that Mount Igman was important geographically and militarily. And he agreed that the Muslim artillery at Mount Igman had Serbian zones in Sarajevo, Nedzarici, Otes, Ilidza, within their range, together with Butmir, Sokolovic Kolonija, and Hrasnica which were Muslim-controlled areas in Sarajevo. That was confirmed on page 5846. So as a result of the majority of the reports -- 5846 is the reference. As a result of the majority of reports which contain qualifications to the effect that in analysing these reports, one must bear in mind that all heavy weapons of both sides were not observed. This he confirmed on page 5847. And that these reports were actually defective or flawed precisely because not all sources of fire were observed. When asked further about the accuracy of the reporting, Lieutenant-Colonel Mole said that the statistics which were seen in the reports was an incorrect representation of the events. It was an attempt to initiate a level of activity. The observers -- the observers were preparing this for the -- or actually, this is in respect of the UN observers. They were just observing a limited, limited number of events and had a limited number of observation posts. So from the testimony of Lieutenant-Colonel Mole we can see for what purposes their reports could be used. They could be only used to actually have a hint of the level of the activity that they performed. They can say nothing about the justification or the activity or the sources of fire or the proportions of the respective activities of heavy weaponry in Sarajevo. This, he says on page 5850. And if it is time for our break, Your Honours. I do have to apologise because I am obviously -- for the accuracy of the interpretation I should speak more slowly, but that of course consumes much of my time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. At this pace, I would not be able to actually say everything that I wish to say. And I will have to condense my presentation because of time constraints. And of course I wish to be precise in respect of the references. Mr. Tucker stated that the Bosnian Presidency had for its objective the re-establishment of territorial integrity and multi-ethnic -- a multi-ethnic community in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a unitary state that had already been recognised, and that is on page -- excuse me --
