utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23240 and 23241 are the pages. However, when cross-examined, on page 23276, he admitted that he drew his information about that when the Prosecutor presented to him, showed to him documents of the army of the Bosnian Serbs and that at that time he had no first-hand knowledge which actually reduces his testimony to just a presentation of his thoughts and his conclusions. Recently, in the case -- in the Mladic case, the Trial Chamber reprimanded or warned several times the Defence not to ask their witnesses questions to which they would reply with their beliefs or their thoughts and that was done in several instances. In this particular case, this Prosecution is basing everything on the beliefs and opinions of witnesses, especially foreign witnesses who were not at all called as expert witnesses but as fact witnesses, and everything that they said were mostly their own convictions. Mr. Banbury, who has been quoted frequently, on pages 13369 and in respect to D1140 also on page 13370 and 13369, he admitted that he did not -- that he had testified to many things which are contrary to his convictions and beliefs; namely, that the Muslim side had actually carried out tricks in order to deceive the international community. And when he was asked, he said that he himself had written such reports. This he admitted on pages 13369 and 70. But of course he failed to put that in his original statement. And as for Banbury, a lot could be said about him and if I have the time I will do so. Banbury does not have an inkling about the mandate of the United Nations. He should have actually trained and instructed the newly arrived officers about the mandate of UNPROFOR. He claimed that the Serbian side had nothing to do with their presence, that there was no approval or consent needed from the Serbian side, but Banbury said that they had come to save the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that when demilitarisation is carried out, all forces are to be withdrawn except government forces. And these are very harmful consequences in the field, and these witnesses were total unusable because they didn't have an idea what they were supposed to do. How can they assess the acts of the Serbs when they always thought that the government, the so-called government, was always right and that the Serbs were the aggressors. This is how things stand. The first ones who came, they knew much more about their mandate; the very next generation didn't know anything about it. For instance, Harland, Harland says, on pages 2058 and 020 -- 206 and so on, that he was the political eyes and ears for the leadership of UNPROFOR which focused on more political than on military issues because, in his own admission, he had no military education to speak of. But he's testifying about imminently military issues although he was not in charge of that nor was duly qualified, competent, for that. His sources of information in respect of military issues were his mere presence where people talked about those issues. So he hears what officers who are experts, who are professionals, say about some military topics or matters and then he testifies about such matters. For instance, he never exchanged a single word with me. He sat in the third row and he took notes; whereas here he speaks about my political views, the objectives of my conference and how much territory I was demanding for the Bosnian Serbs. And this is something he has no way of knowing because he was not at any of the peace conferences. Only Akashi or Cutileiro or Owen can be asked about those things, those people who were given my requests in that respect and were presented our positions vis-à-vis these matters. The Prosecution uses Banbury and Harland to state views on matters which they do not know anything about nor could have known anything about nor should have testified about. He collected information from a number of sources, including the UNMOs, the value of which we have already seen demonstrated and which is seriously challenged by the commanders of the United Nations, Rose, Briquemont as well, I believe. I believe that all of them said that they were good for nothing. And he also ventured to characterise the events, he drew up reports, daily -- drafts of daily and weekly reports, and the final conclusions depended not exclusively on what had happened in reality to the highest degree, but on the balance of influences of the nations which actually provided the observers. And he speaks about this on page 20 -- 2067. And on 2066, he admitted that he believed that the logs, the diaries, of his superiors were, after all, more reliable than his own views and than his own testimonies. He also testified that his reports created day after day were based -- as well as his weekly reports were based on seven-day compilations from different sources, from a variety of sources without a uniform methodology, so it was accumulated without a single methodology, so one piece of information could feature a number of times in a single report. There were no investigations, particularly not in the criminal law sense. But the testimony of Mr. Harland was even of lesser importance and lesser utility because in his reports he manifestly showed himself to be partial. As he said in his own words, he was there to defend the government and the measures and the agreements did not apply to the government forces. So there you have it. That is on page 2066, as well as in his amalgamated statements, paragraphs 31 through 33. The most dubious segment of his theory of shelling Sarajevo emanates from -- which would have no military purpose and would represent actually the base of terror, his sweeping statements are not based on a single investigation, not even on superficial knowledge of legitimate military targets and the disposition of forces in Sarajevo, in particular the disposition of the forces of the 1st Corps which outnumbered the SRK forces three times. Harland admitted that he only had some general knowledge, and this he did on page -- that is in the Krstic case on page 2351 and 2304 where he said -- in our case it was 2352. And 2352 is the page reference in our case. He says that he had only general knowledge, and on page 2304 he admitted that it was correct. I'll read out his sentence. [In English] "It is true that there were Bosnian gun positions rather close. The city of Sarajevo is highly compact." [Interpretation] Similar testimony was provided by General Dzambasovic, that they could not remove their artillery pieces from the residential area because the city was small. Well, they could have accepted demilitarisation and then there wouldn't have been any problem whatsoever. Also, it would have sufficed if they had not fired, opened fire, then nothing would have happened. Corwin, another representative of the UN, was threatened, he received death threats because of his reporting in his own way. And that is D1169. It was the Muslim side that was issuing these threats because they were not happy with his reporting. When we recall that General Morillon explained why he was not reporting on Muslim crimes, he said: Well, we have to live here. D717, the Memorandum of Understanding between UNPROFOR and Republika Srpska in respect of the total exclusion zone, D717. It confirms the right of the Serb side to use their weapons when they're attacked. Van Lynden, a journalist, he testified on 2422, that's the page reference. He said that it was possible that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had sniper positions on the Holiday Inn, on government buildings, and the museum. Further on he testified that when the war started - this is page 2342 - that there were no Muslim troops in Sarajevo. However, as Sefer Halilovic, a general of the Muslim army, said, the forces of the Territorial Defence included 16 municipal centres of the Territorial Defence, 16 units of the Territorial Defence, about 500 independent units, 450 independent groups, and 100 anti-sabotage units. In response to a question that was put to him, Witness Van Lynden continued to deny such a military presence in Sarajevo. 2454 is the page reference. General Halilovic confirmed that the Muslim soldiers wore civilian clothes, that they started conflicts. That is 2465-7, that's the page reference. Van Lynden on page 2461, 62, says that -- the previous reference, General Halilovic, when he confirmed that civilians -- or rather, his soldiers were wearing civilian clothes and they started attacks, that is 2456, 57. Van Lynden confirmed that he did not receive information concerning active operations of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, 2461 and 62 are the page references for that. 2461 to 2462. And the previous one was 2456 to 57. Also on page 2467 he confirmed that he was aware, that he knew, that the number of troops had a 2:1 ratio in favour of the Muslim side. On page 2461 he said that he never saw a tank in Sarajevo. Under Muslim control, that is. On page 2472 through 73, Van Lynden agreed that, generally speaking, there were legitimate targets in town located on the hill of Hum at least. Van Lynden, on page 2473 through 74, confirmed that the buildings of Unis, the government buildings, Treska, et cetera, were used for military purposes. We saw what he presented as evidence here, that is to say, his very own montage on the television that he worked for as if it were live coverage. These strange tracer shells are seen in the background and he admitted to us that this was edited, that it was a montage, although he presented it differently to his viewers. That poor guy, he had exposed himself to danger, that he was under fire as he was reporting. He had to agree -- actually, notes were shown to him -- no, state security from 1992, stating that the Green Berets had taken over the Hotel Evropa in the old town, then the Zagreb Hotel and so on. In his reports, Van Lynden did not say who it was that was firing at who. However, he left the impression that it was Serbs that were firing at town and that is the impression he wanted to create. Although there was gun-fire right in front of the military hospital where he was. Around the military hospital there were Muslim mortars, there was a howitzer above the military hospital, and he did not report about and he confirmed that on 2494. He did not say who was firing at who, but the context clearly suggested that it was the wild Serbs who were firing at the tame Sarajevo. On page 2501 and 2511, he confirmed that the Green Berets made Van Lynden's stay at the hotel or at hotels impossible because their presence at the Bristol Hotel at the square of Pero Kosoric made it unpleasant, so that's probably why he was at the military hospital. I want to save time so that will do as far as Van Lynden is concerned. And then on all these pages up until 2619, Van Lynden is contradictory. He's more of a propagandist and the most that he could do was to say -- not to say who was firing at who because the conclusion would be that it was the Serbs. Jeremy Bowen is one of the reporters who said that snipers were probably Serb and that they fired at a bus that was coming from the direction of the Bosnian government building and that fire was opened then, on page 10150. He came to that conclusion through a process of elimination because of the weight of indirect evidence, 10151 is the page reference. He admits that he was lying about the position of the Serb gunners, the Bosnian Serb gunners, on the Oslobodjenje building because he did not know that at the time -- because physically -- actually, he admitted that he was not there physically and that he -- or rather, that it was impossible to fire from there. Jeremy Bowen deduces that the Bosnian Serbs are responsible for the shelling of the cemetery Lav because that was regular shelling of that cemetery and he said that that was within the range of Serb weaponry. 10182 is the page reference. Also he says that it was not in the range of the Muslim weapons. Martin Bell testified as well, on the 22nd of April, paramilitary groups, the Green Berets, attacked the headquarters of the 2nd Military District in Sarajevo. 9815 and 16 are the page references. On Serb territory in Ilidza, Muslim groups attacked the Serbs at the same time, around the 22nd of April, that is, 9818-19. Bell agreed that that Muslim armed groups did exist in town. Martin Bell agreed that secret directives were issued to Muslim soldiers, that they should momentarily take weapons from the arms depot in order to cut off the barracks there, to take them prisoner throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is on page 9829 through 30. Armed groups of Muslims were also present at Vrace in the Serb neighbourhood. Martin Bell was aware that the Muslims were very skilful in concealing their weapons as UN weapons. Sometimes he would come across mortars or he would see mortars, and that was a very sensitive question on the ground. 9863 is the page reference, when he said that journalists saw this for themselves, they saw this mortar fire, and had they reported about that they would have suffered consequences. The Muslim forces did have heavy weapons in and around Sarajevo. The Bosnian forces -- no, the Serb forces clashed at two fronts with the Muslim forces. That is 9864. He confirmed that Mojmilo is dominant on 9865, that's a dominant position in Muslim hands. He confirmed that the forces of the Presidency discovered how wide-ranging this Muslim operation was, about 500 independent platoons and squads were concealed from the media and the UN. 9869 through 70, that's the page reference. On page 9898 he confirmed that there were military installations, military infrastructure in town, and that they manufactured weapons and ammunition, and that, ironically, the Serbs were in a subordinate position with the heavy weapons because the Muslim forces were carrying out attacks with the intention of causing a reaction. 9902 is the page reference. All this information that is objective and that is favourable for the Defence was received only in cross-examination. The Prosecution did not make an effort, was not interested in painting the entire picture for the Trial Chamber. They only portrayed a partial picture to the detriment of the Serbs. Also, that was not reflected in their reports to their media companies, although there were some indications of editors cutting it out even if they did include it in their reports. Martin Bell was aware that in Hrasnica there were 4.500 Muslim soldiers in the 4th Motorised Brigade on page 9903. On page 9909, he was not surprised that command posts of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were deployed in residential areas so as not to be targeted, whereas they could fire from there. Bell was aware of that, he knew that the forces of the Bosnian Muslims, of the Bosnian government as he says, such as the 14th and 16th Divisions were part of the 1st Corps and that they were located in Tarcin, or rather, in the northern part of Sarajevo. He speaks about that on page 9910 and 991 -- no, 9910 through 12. He confirms that the balance of power was shifting in the territory of Sarajevo, that the Muslims had enormous forces in a relatively small territory. He also confirmed that Izetbegovic declared general mobilisation on the 4th of April. Martin Bell confirmed a few things that have to do with Karadzic's conduct that work in favour of the Defence. Again, this was stated in response to questions put by the Defence. If I have enough time, I'm going to show that as well. The Muslim forces are also a significant source of information for the OTP, for building up their case in relation to Sarajevo. Ekrem Suljevic testified and quite a bit of the Prosecution case is based on his testimony and his findings that projectiles mostly came from the positions on the Serb side. When he was asked about the reasons concerning shells coming from the Serb side, he simply said the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina would not shoot at its own people. So that would not have been possible, it couldn't be ascribed to them that they were shelling their own people. 5788 is the page reference, 290, and that is the page reference where he determined the source or origin of fire on the base of this analogy, this inference, that the Muslim side would not fire. He was asked to determine the type of shell and calibre in his investigations and the direction from which the shell came. What he established was not conducive to any exact information. During the trial, Suljevic testified about the procedures employed in these investigations on page 5741 to 5742, and he said that he relied on ballistics reports as to whether a bomb was detonated on page 5744, and the velocity of projectile and other information was included in these reports. The witness based his findings on a balance of probabilities and he testified about that on page 5755 to 57. A photograph of Safet Hadzic Street is one of the exhibits and that exhibit is D533. This photograph does not depict either the impact or the damage. There are no traces of detonation. Page 5790 to 97. Further on, on pages 6151 and on, the witness claims that projectiles came from the aggressor, that is to say, the Serb side, without any efforts to determine the origin or any references to the confrontation line in that zone, and he did not in any way rule out the possibility that the shell came from Muslim positions. Crucial information such as the angle of impact, angle of descent, and exact location are totally absent from his reports. Irregularities regarding fragments are constant and they remain for the most part outside of the scope of his report and the witness provided no further explanation. That's page 6180 to 6195, and 6206. There are no reports on fragments. There is no indication that fragments were investigated and analysed. That's pages 5723 to 24, 5733, 5739, 5746 and 47. The witness testified that he was not a ballistics expert. Referring to "our" reports, not his own report, he confirmed that he never participated in drafting reports done by his section. Instead, it was his colleagues who drafted them but he came to testify instead of these colleagues. Asked about a particular report on page 6217 to 6219 and 6158 to 6159, in several cases the witness said he was totally not responsible for any flaws in the report, saying that he did not write it, saying that he was an ordinary member of the team, despite the fact that he had been involved in these investigations. Mirsad Agic [as interpreted], another investigator, together with his team leader, Dragan Jokovic, on page T7752, the report was submitted without a ballistics report. And Mirza Sabljica confirmed that the information in the report was unreliable. In addition, the investigations did not reveal the exact location of the origin of fire or the distance or the direction of fire with any accuracy. So the findings do not enable any conclusions. On pages 7745 to 46, regarding reports on trams, the tram was put back in the position where it was hit, according to the witness, in order to determine where the projectile came into contact with the vehicle. The witness said it was crucial and could give a totally different picture of the incident. Regarding incident F14, on page 7887, his crime investigation department was not able to determine where automatic fire came from on the Serbian side without referring to ballistics reports; however, that's precisely what they did, they made conclusions without consulting ballistics reports. Furthermore, because the tram was not in its original position as when it was hit, they did not determine the exact location, and he says that on page 7889. Regarding the incident on Livanjska Street, which is not part of this case, Sabljica agreed that it was not investigated by an investigating judge; page 7748 and 49. None of the directions discussed with this witness regarding G6 is the location from which a projectile was fired at the institute in Butmir. Regarding incident G6, applying the method that was available to them, one could only determine in general terms that it was fired from the west. This location, the Institute for Blind Children that Sabljica marked, is not south-west from -- no, it is south-west to the place of impact, not north-west. And it is more likely that it came from different locations such as the students' hostels; that's pages 7808 and 09. Regarding G9, the direction of fire was determined during the investigation but the angle of descent was not. Mirza Sabljica was asked not to investigate on the following day despite the need for a ballistics finding. That's on page 7915. Sabljica also claims, on pages 7752 and 53, 7762 and 7106, that he was totally unaware that his team leader denied access to the UNPROFOR, and that without the knowledge of this witness he submitted his report the very same day and that report did not include the findings of Mirza Sabljica. That's on pages 7752 and 53, pages 7762 and 7106. Ballistics report reveal that the azimuth was to the south-east rather -- correction, to the north-east rather than north. And that was not standard practice according to the evidence of this witness. He shifted responsibility to forensic technicians who, according to him, made a mistake. That's pages 7763 and 64. On page T8224, Bogdan Vidovic testified that the origin of fire was never determined. Nothing, save for a general direction. The angle of descent was possible to determine but it was not determined and it was not included in the report. Regarding incident F8, this witness, Bogdan Vidovic, has no clue about which direction the fire came and the investigation only determined a general direction from which it could have come. The assumption was that it was on the Bosnian Serb side, and based on that assumption they determined the trajectory, instead of first determining the trajectory and then the rest. It's on pages 8174 to 76 and 8191. Concerning the distance from the confrontation line, Bogdan Vidovic said he knew nothing about that zone and he could only speculate. But despite that, despite the fact that he had only general knowledge about the direction of fire, his report does state which side is to blame. In one of the incidents, a photograph used as evidence reveals where the bullet impacted on the tram and where it hit the seats. Judging by the height of impact and the angle at which it travelled, these indicators were not taken into account. That was established on page 8193. The investigation did not establish whether fire was accidental or deliberate. And during his testimony, the witness did not rule out this possibility, that it was accidental. On page 8193 and 96, it was established that traces were found in the tram and bullet casings were found in the tram, but the witness didn't know which side used which type of bullets. That's on page 8196.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the number of the incident.

utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat the number of that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The date of the incident is 14 February 1995. It is an F incident. I'll look up the number. It could be 94. I'm not sure. It's not even in the indictment, although it could be. It was sufficient for them to have established the direction as if there were not both forces at the position from which it was fired and at the impact site. But in their own admission, the investigating organs in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and this was actually admitted by a witness in respect of the investigation in Dobrinja on the 4th of February - so they did not conduct investigations during the war the way they would have done and they did before the war which they could present before a court of law. Can we now take the break because I'll trying to abridge this, to condense it, because I have very much to present yet.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. They never heard about the units, battalions, companies, brigades, of that army. They never heard about the staffs of the army. Almir Begic, for instance, did hear that the Deltas did have a staff in Velesici, and simply they are not of any use as witnesses. Almir Begic demonstrated how unusable he is as a witness on pages 9982 to 85, 9979 to 80, 9985, 9986, 9988 to 89, 9989, 11750, 11751, 11752, 11765, 11766, 11763, 11764, and 11771. From Velesici to his unit in the centre of Sarajevo at Bjelave, he passed via one route every day, and all the streets in Sarajevo were available for the manoeuvring, coming and going, and supply of the units for their rotation, for their shifts, and all these were legitimate targets which were very infrequently targeted. And they were fired on, according to the testimonies of the commanders of the Sarajevo brigades, only in order to prevent, postpone, or discourage them from attacking. Alen Gicevic, also a witness for the Prosecution, either did not know about or he lied about facts associated with legitimate military targets in Sarajevo as can be seen on the following pages: 7630, 7636, 7638, 7628 to 30, 7632 to 34, 7648, 7659 to 60, 7662 to 63, 7639 to 40, 7653, 7655. Irrespective of the fact whether a witness doesn't know, didn't know, when it was deliberately lying, the testimony of such a witness is of no use. If he doesn't know where the forces are, if he doesn't know who is shooting at whom or doesn't want to know, then such a witness -- the testimony of such a validity has to be taken into due consideration without any moral condemnation whether he is a mendacious witness or not. So Dr. Youssef Hajir, he said very nice things about the accused, that he was proud that he knew him, et cetera, either didn't know or he lied, and the Defence believes that he didn't know, he was not aware of some facts related to legitimate military targets in Sarajevo as can be seen on pages 8843, 8825, 8847, 8849, 8850, 8812 to 3, 8820, 8819, 8823. Fahra Mujanovic either did not know or lied about facts related to legitimate military targets that she could see. And that is in evidence on the following pages: 8750, 8794, 8751, 8768, 8764 to 65, 8761 to 62, 8766, 8762. It is not probable - in fact, it is not possible - that she didn't know that in her own hamlet that she testified about as having come under fire, that there was a staff there and a mortar battery located in that hamlet. That cannot be. Bakir Nakas either didn't know or lied about facts associated with legitimate military targets in Sarajevo as seen in the following pages. It is hard to believe that somebody doesn't know that behind the military hospital in which he was working there were mortar batteries shooting or that at Gorica, above the military hospital, there was a howitzer emplacement. Bakir Nakas is the witness. This is in evidence that -- namely that his testimony was flawed, and that can be seen on pages 6700 to 1, 6744, 6745, 6746, 6702 to 03, 6703, 6708, 6709, 6710, 6711, 6743. Alma Mulaosmanovic either did not know or she lied about facts related to legitimate military targets and events in Sarajevo. And that can be seen on pages 6753, 6762, 6764, 6766 to 7, and 9779. And another Trial Chamber in the General Milosevic case concluded this, and I believe it was paragraph 352. UNPROFOR reported that there was an exchange of fire around Vrbanja. The Army of Republika Srpska claimed that there had been an exchange of fire and the observers also confirmed that there was -- that there was an exchange of fire, but Alma said that there was no exchange of fire. She was sitting in a tram and she only passed through the zone in which fire was being opened for 20 seconds. And the Trial Chamber actually relied on what Alma said, that there had been no exchange of fire. She was hit by a bullet from another burst. We heard her, she testified here. So this bullet came from another burst of fire. It was obvious that she had not been the target and that it had not been sniper fire, but that paragraph remains on account of which General Milosevic got a few years. Fatima Zaimovic, one of the witnesses among the inhabitants of Sarajevo, was not aware of or lied about facts associated with legitimate military targets in Sarajevo and this is on the following pages. Let me just remind you, this is the lady witness, she saw from Breka on Osmice a cannon opening fire, she saw the shell coming out of the barrel and travelling through air and such other hilarious things and she failed to see a tank which was just 50 metres away from her house at Breka. She didn't know that her son was a member of the 105th Brigade, which was a very powerful, very well-equipped brigade in Sarajevo, and held Breka. So Fatima Zaimovic, the wife of a friend of mine from my youth as matter of fact, was shown not to tell the truth on pages 1898 to 9, 1891, 1904 to 05, 1908 to 10, 1963 to 4, 1966, 1975 to 81, 1989 to 90, 1990 to 1, so 1990 to 1, 2002 to 3, 1928 to 9, 1910, 1929 to 1930. So many, many facts that discredit this witness, though her testimony was short. Milan Mandilovic either did not know or lied about facts related to legitimate military targets in Sarajevo. He had to know about this, and this became obvious on the following pages of the transcript: 5374, 5378, 5384, 5435, 5382, 5385, 5389, 5424, and 5440 through 3. So many things, not knowing so many things and yet testifying. This shows how useless all that testimony is in a criminal case. Of course, none of that was obvious on the basis of amalgamated statements. The Defence had to exert pressure and to squeeze this out of them because of all the contradictions and all the ludicrous statements that we heard. Not to mention other witnesses like Eset Muracevic, who smuggled shells across the lines and when he was arrested he wondered why he had been arrested. Quite simply, it is to be expected, the Defence hopes that the Trial Chamber is going to double-check each and every allegation made and that they're not going to take anything at face value. Since there is one more witness left, I'd like to ask that we move into private session for a few minutes so that we can indicate the essence of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we go into private session, line 15 an previous page should read "Zaimovic" and line 20 should read "Mandilovic."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Excellency.
